method_card.title: How to Estimate Gradients of Curves & Areas Under Graphs
method_card.content:
To estimate the gradient of a curve at a point, draw a tangent (a straight line that just touches the curve at that point). Then find the gradient of the tangent using rise ÷ run.

To estimate the area under a curve, use the trapezium rule or count squares. The trapezium rule splits the area into strips:

$$A \approx \frac{h}{2}\left[y_0 + y_n + 2(y_1 + y_2 + \ldots + y_{n-1})\right]$$

where \(h\) is the strip width and \(y_0, y_1, \ldots, y_n\) are the y-values at each boundary.

In real-life contexts: the gradient of a distance-time graph at a point gives instantaneous speed; the area under a speed-time curve gives distance.
method_card.example:
Estimate the area under \(y = x^2\) from \(x = 0\) to \(x = 4\) using 4 strips.

Strip width \(h = 1\). Values: \(y_0 = 0, y_1 = 1, y_2 = 4, y_3 = 9, y_4 = 16\)

$$A \approx \frac{1}{2}[0 + 16 + 2(1 + 4 + 9)] = \frac{1}{2}[16 + 28] = 22$$

gold.display: Use the trapezium rule with 5 strips (\(h = 1\)) and y-values 1, 2, 5, 10, 17, 26. Estimate the area.
The area under a speed-time curve from \(t = 0\) to \(t = 10\) is estimated as 85 m using the trapezium rule. The exact area is 83 m. Is the trapezium rule an overestimate or underestimate?

misconceptions.message: 85 > 83 so it's an overestimate. For curves that are concave up, the trapezium rule overestimates.

Explain why using more strips in the trapezium rule gives a better estimate. What happens to the accuracy as the number of strips increases?
options: Accuracy increases — strips better approximate the curve
Accuracy depends on the curve shape only

misconceptions.message: More strips = narrower strips = each trapezium fits the curve more closely = better approximation.
